metadata.file_name: J Educational Measurement - 2026 - Xue - Evaluating General‐Purpose Multimodal AI for Q‐Matrix Generation from Math Items .pdf
metadata.title: Evaluating General‐Purpose Multimodal AI for Q‐Matrix Generation from Math Items: A Cognitive Diagnostic Modeling Exploration

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2007, TIMSS 2011, and PISA 2012 mathematics item response data to evaluate AI-generated Q-matrices via cognitive diagnostic model fitting and Q-matrix matching. The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or any replicate-weight procedures, and it does not name any weight variables from the underlying TIMSS/PISA datasets. Because the analysis is centered on Q-matrix generation and subsequent CDM model fitting (rather than estimating population-representative achievement distributions), the paper provides no explicit weighting strategy; therefore, weighting cannot be confirmed from the text. The analytic inputs appear to be the specified item sets and the corresponding student response datasets used in the CDM R package, with no additional sample filtering criteria described beyond the dataset/task selection.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study does not analyze PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes; instead, it generates and validates Q-matrices (item–attribute mappings) and evaluates them using CDM fit indices (AIC, BIC, log-likelihood, SRMSR) and Q-matrix matching/discrepancy metrics. Because the dependent variables are not PV-based achievement scores, PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data strategy for the student response data used in the CDM R package, so the missing-data handling approach is a reporting gap.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses (a) TIMSS 2007 and TIMSS 2011 mathematics item sets (25 items for TIMSS 07; 26 items for TIMSS 11) with response data provided via the CDM R package, and (b) PISA 2012 mathematics items administered across four regions (Shanghai, Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan) with expert-calibrated Q-matrices as benchmarks. For TIMSS, the Q-matrix candidates are specified from prior research (TIMSS 07 uses the matrix as the true value; TIMSS 11 uses four candidate true Q-matrices). For PISA 2012, the expert-generated Q-matrix is treated as the benchmark and the student response data are used to validate model fit and matching. Beyond these dataset/item/region selections, the manuscript does not report additional inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., missing response exclusions, response-time filters, or complete-case criteria).

main_findings.target_variable: CDM model fit quality using AI-generated Q-matrices
main_findings.performance_metrics: For DINA: SRMSR Human 0.0739 vs Gemini-2.5-pro all-at-once 0.0662 (AIC 77711.83, BIC 226970.74, log-likelihood -5903.91). For RRUM: SRMSR Human 0.0601 vs Gemini-2.5-pro all-at-once 0.0615 (AIC 76749.12, BIC 226174.48, log-likelihood -5512.56). For LLM: SRMSR Human 0.0620 vs Gemini-2.5-pro all-at-once 0.0593 (AIC 76892.54, BIC 226310.17, log-likelihood -5562.27). Additional analysis (Chatbot-human Q-matrix matching (unsupervised matching accuracy)): Best reported: Gemini-2.5-pro (all-at-once) matching rate 0.891; precision 0.872; F1-score 0.624; G-mean 0.691. ChatGPT-4o (one-by-one) matching rate 0.867; precision 0.763; F1-score 0.537; G-mean 0.634. Claude-sonnet-4 (all-at-once) matching rate 0.875; precision 0.829; F1-score 0.552; G-mean 0.637.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2007 Mathematics the study leveraged AI-generated Q-matrix structure (via different LLMs and prompting modes) to predict CDM model fit quality, finding that AI-generated Q-matrices often improved fit indices (e.g., lower AIC/BIC and lower SRMSR such as DINA SRMSR 0.0662 vs 0.0739 for Gemini-2.5-pro all-at-once). This indicates that LLM-generated Q-matrices can provide empirically adequate item–attribute mappings for cognitive diagnostic modeling, enabling faster Q-matrix development without sacrificing residual-based fit.

main_findings.target_variable: CDM model fit quality using AI-generated Q-matrices
main_findings.performance_metrics: For GDINA: SRMSR Human 0.0521–0.0620 vs Gemini-2.5-pro all-at-once 0.0721 (AIC 83628.93, BIC 245101.79, log-likelihood -8979.46) and Claude-sonnet-4 all-at-once 0.0602 (AIC 83789.51, BIC 245632.17, log-likelihood -8994.75). For DINA: SRMSR Human 0.0719–0.0922 vs ChatGPT-4o all-at-once 0.0804 (AIC 74497.97, BIC 199575.81, log-likelihood -4429.99). For LLM: SRMSR Human 0.0612–0.0673 vs Gemini-2.5-pro all-at-once 0.0595 (AIC 73498.67, BIC 198549.26, log-likelihood -3881.34). Additional analysis (Chatbot-human Q-matrix matching (unsupervised matching accuracy)): Best reported: ChatGPT-4o (one-by-one) matching rate 0.905 (SE 0.011); precision 0.861 (SE 0.011); F1-score 0.630 (SE 0.024); G-mean 0.700 (SE 0.023). Gemini-2.5-pro (all-at-once) matching rate 0.892 (SE 0.013); precision 0.818 (SE 0.000); F1-score 0.567 (SE 0.029); G-mean 0.653 (SE 0.026). Claude-sonnet-4 (one-by-one) matching rate 0.799 (SE 0.010); precision 0.301 (SE 0.012); F1-score 0.231 (SE 0.004); G-mean 0.415 (SE 0.009).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 Mathematics the study leveraged AI-generated Q-matrices to predict CDM model fit quality, finding that SRMSR values for AI-generated matrices remained within acceptable thresholds and that several AI variants achieved competitive or improved fit indices relative to human baselines (e.g., LLM SRMSR 0.0595 for Gemini-2.5-pro all-at-once vs human 0.0612–0.0673). This indicates that even when AI outputs differ in sparsity from experts, they can still support adequate cognitive diagnostic model estimation for larger assessments.

main_findings.target_variable: CDM model fit quality using AI-generated Q-matrices
main_findings.performance_metrics: For DINA: SRMSR Human 0.0213 vs Claude-sonnet-4 all-at-once 0.0129 (AIC 74622.99, BIC 75480.33, log-likelihood -37189.49) and Gemini-2.5-pro all-at-once 0.0154 (AIC 74645.77, BIC 75462.18, log-likelihood -37180.89). For GDINA: SRMSR Human 0.0208 vs Claude-sonnet-4 all-at-once 0.0120 (AIC 74511.00, BIC 75346.03, log-likelihood -37132.50). For LLM: SRMSR Human 0.0201 vs Claude-sonnet-4 all-at-once 0.0121 (AIC 74611.22, BIC 75473.66, log-likelihood -37186.61). Additional analysis (Chatbot-human Q-matrix matching (unsupervised matching accuracy)): Best reported: Claude-sonnet-4 (all-at-once) matching rate 0.889; precision 0.846; F1-score 0.846; G-mean 0.879. Gemini-2.5-pro (one-by-one) matching rate 0.833; precision 0.769; F1-score 0.769; G-mean 0.818. ChatGPT-4o (all-at-once) matching rate 0.819; precision 0.741; F1-score 0.755; G-mean 0.808.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study leveraged AI-generated Q-matrices to predict CDM model fit quality, finding that AI variants—especially Claude-sonnet-4 under all-at-once prompting—produced substantially low SRMSR values and competitive AIC/BIC/log-likelihood compared with the human benchmark (e.g., DINA SRMSR 0.0129 vs 0.0213). This indicates that LLM-based Q-matrix generation can yield empirically strong CDM inputs for smaller item sets, supporting broader adoption of diagnostic measurement workflows.

data.outcome_summary: This study evaluates multimodal LLMs (ChatGPT-4o, Claude-sonnet-4, Gemini-2.5-pro) as an Attribute-based Automatic Q-Matrix Generator for cognitive diagnostic modeling. It uses TIMSS 2007 (25 items; 698 students), TIMSS 2011 (26 items; 1,010 students), and PISA 2012 mathematics items (6 attributes; 12 items; 6,561 students across Shanghai, Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan) to compare AI-generated Q-matrices against expert benchmarks. Across datasets, AI-generated Q-matrices show strong chatbot-human matching accuracy (e.g., TIMSS 2011 best matching rate 0.905 with precision 0.861 and F1 0.630; PISA 2012 best precision/F1 0.846 with G-mean 0.879). In exploratory CDM fit analyses using DINA, DINO, RRUM, GDINA, and LLM, AI-generated matrices often achieve competitive or improved AIC/BIC/log-likelihood and consistently low SRMSR values, indicating adequate residual-based fit. Limitations include the absence of reported survey-weighting and missing-data handling, and the fact that Q-matrix fidelity is assessed via matching and fit indices rather than causal effects on learning outcomes.
